source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Founding GJP design. Forecasters were randomly assigned to training, teaming and tracking conditions in a 2-year IARPA tournament. The top 2% of Year 1 were placed in elite teams in Year 2.
numbers: Year 1: 2,246 participants (1,593 survey, 653 market traders), about 177 per condition, attrition 7%. Year 2: 1,648 participants, attrition 3%. Entry needed a degree plus a 2-hour test battery. 76% US, 83% male, mean age 36, 64% postgraduate. Pay $150 (Y1), $250 (Y2), not tied to accuracy.
limits: Volunteer, educated, mostly male sample. Year 2 'no training' group included some Year 1 scenario-trained people, which biases against finding a training effect.
agent_relevance: Our agent has no stable person to track, but the design shows what to randomize: instruction, interaction, and selection of the best.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Superforecasters showed no regression to the mean in Year 2. They beat every other group by a wide margin. This is the founding persistence result.
numbers: Year 2 Table 1 mean Brier by window (first week / middle 2 weeks / last week): superforecasters .25/.19/.07; regular teams, no training .38/.32/.16; untrained individuals .46/.39/.26. Superforecasters answered 95 questions vs 61 for regular teams, t(270)=6.88; made 7.8 forecasts per question vs 1.6 for teams.
quote: There was no evidence of Year 2 regression to the mean; political forecasting appeared to be at least somewhat skill based
limits: Selected on one year, tested on new questions, but they also got team support at the same time. So persistence and the team boost are mixed. Brier here is the 0-2 scale version.
agent_relevance: Skill is partly stable AND effort-driven. Superforecasters updated about 5 times more often. A scaffold should copy the updating habit, not just the label.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: A short probability training module helped in both years. Probability training beat scenario training, and both beat no training.
numbers: Y1 training F(2,1586)=14.29; prob vs scenario t(1053)=2.23 p=.026; scenario vs none t(1056)=3.25. Y2 prob vs none F(1,882)=19.12 p<.001. Module took about 45 minutes; benefit lasted across periods of 8 to 10 months. Table 1 Y1 last-week Brier: individuals none .31, prob .29; teams none .22, prob .19.
quote: a brief probabilistic training module paid off over an extended time
limits: Training effect could be confounded by self-selected questions; scores were standardized within question to control this.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level 'training' (base rates, reference classes, averaging) is the cheapest lever. Matches the outside view guidance.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Teaming beat crowd-belief polling, which beat independent forecasting. This contradicts the claim that independence is best. Team members shared news and rationales.
numbers: Y1 group F(2,1586)=60.68; team vs crowd-belief t(1036)=5.52; crowd vs independent t(1120)=5.92. Y2 F(1,882)=62.76. Comments per member correlated with accuracy r=-.19 (Y1), -.22 (Y2) (lower Brier is better). Untrained independents were the worst. Teams attempted fewer questions than individuals.
limits: Teams had a norm of sharing and were not anonymous crowds. Groupthink was not found but not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Single agent: interaction is replaced by structured self-critique. Note G4 in our schema: same-model copies are not independent, so team gains may not transfer.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Calibration and resolution both improved with training, teaming and tracking. Superforecasters gained mostly through resolution (decisiveness). Forecasters were overconfident, worst at 100%.
numbers: Calibration: training F(2,1586)=3.16, p=.04; superforecasters vs trained teams t(293)=11.03. Resolution: group Y1 F(2,1586)=78.53; training F(2,1586)=18.50; tracking t(293)=4.12. Forecasts of 100% made in the first 20% of a question's life were right only about 70%; in the last 20%, about 90%.
limits: Binary questions only in the calibration plots. Overconfidence at the extremes was due to a lack of updating.
agent_relevance: Good forecasters are sharp AND calibrated. Our agent must be able to move to extremes late (resolution), not hedge at 50%.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions
finding: Companion paper to the 2014 one, and the main source for persistence and trait correlates. I could not get the full text. What I know comes from its abstract and from AI Impacts and Himmelstein 2021 summaries of it.
numbers: Abstract: superforecasters kept high accuracy over hundreds of questions across 2 years. AI Impacts reports a structural model with multiple correlation .64 using dispositional, situational and behavioral variables (second-hand).
limits: NOT READ. Numbers are second-hand. Do not cite exact trait correlations from here.
agent_relevance: Four explanations given: abilities and styles, task skills, motivation, enriched environment. Needs a re-fetch if full text can be reached.

source: AI Impacts (undated) Evidence on good forecasting practices from the Good Judgment Project
finding: This is the source of the .65 and 70% figures in our subfield row. The page gives them as coming from the book Superforecasting p104, not from a paper with a table. Treat them as popular-book numbers.
numbers: About 70% of superforecasters kept status from one year to the next. Correlation between a forecaster's performance in one year and the next: .65 (across all forecasters). Good-practice ranking puts 'past performance in same domain' first. Reference-class tagged answers averaged Brier .17 vs .26 for the next-best tag (from Chang 2016). GJP beat the control by more than 60%, and beat an intelligence-community prediction market by 25-30% (as reported there).
quote: Roughly 70% of the superforecasters maintained their status from one year to the next
limits: Secondary, blog-level. The .65 is probably a correlation of average scores, not a Brier-based test-retest on matched questions. A footnote says one expert thinks the extremizing success was a fluke. Volunteers throttle down effort, which lowers retention.
agent_relevance: Persistence is real but about 70% (so 30% fall out); do not assume a fixed ranking. For an agent: re-test configurations, do not freeze a 'best' prompt on one season.

source: Himmelstein, Atanasov & Budescu (2021) Forecasting forecaster accuracy: Contributions of past performance and individual differences
finding: Independent test of persistence in the later IARPA Hybrid Forecasting Competition (SAGE group). Split-half correlation of the same accuracy metric across two question sets was only moderate, about .36 to .41. Far below the book figure of .65.
numbers: Season 1: 326 core forecasters, 188 questions, split 94/94. Table 2 same-metric across halves: simple .36, hierarchical .41, IRT .36 (within-time correlations between metrics .71-.83). Season 2: 547 MTurk forecasters, 398 questions.
limits: Metrics differ (normalized accuracy, not mean standardized Brier). Volunteers in S1, paid MTurk in S2. Half-split sets are only 94 questions.
agent_relevance: Single-season skill reliability is modest. For our agent: rank configurations on many questions or the ranking is mostly noise.

source: Himmelstein, Atanasov & Budescu (2021) Forecasting forecaster accuracy: Contributions of past performance and individual differences
finding: Past performance quickly beats psychometric traits as a predictor of future accuracy. After as few as 20 resolved questions, past performance dominated, and it kept adding up to 80.
numbers: Season 1 dominance analysis, n=216 on questions 81-188. IRT model R2 about .57 with 80 questions resolved (Season 2: R2 .35 at 80 and .53 at 200 questions; hierarchical .48; simple .41). Out-of-sample Season 1: n=202 forecasters, 64 test questions.
limits: R2 grows more slowly in S2 because of fewer forecasts per question. Out-of-sample sets are small.
agent_relevance: For a thinking schema: if you can measure results on 20+ cases, trust that over a trait guess (like model size).

source: Himmelstein, Atanasov & Budescu (2021) Forecasting forecaster accuracy: Contributions of past performance and individual differences
finding: Traits that predict accuracy in HFC match GJP. Intelligence, cognitive style, domain knowledge and education had the highest correlations, but they are small (about .1 to .2). Actively open-minded thinking and political knowledge failed in Season 2.
numbers: Table 3 (S1, n=326): CRT about .20, Number Series .15, Berlin Numeracy .15, Matrix Reasoning .15, AOT .15, Need for Cognition .15, political knowledge .11, overconfidence -.15, education .13, age -.07. S2 (n=547) reliabilities: Number Series .77, Berlin Numeracy .66, AOT .24, political knowledge 0; individual-difference model R2 = .11.
limits: Low reliability in S2 explains part of the null. S1 found CRT highest, not Matrix Reasoning as in Mellers 2015.
agent_relevance: Trait-like gains are small (r about .15); active open-mindedness as a rule for the agent has weaker evidence than past results suggest.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers & Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy
finding: Training effect replicated in each of four tournament years (RCTs), with smaller effects later. CHAMPS KNOW training took under one hour.
numbers: Improvement in Brier over control: Y1 10% (probability) and 11% (scenario), n=119/113 vs 152; Y2 12%, t(395)=5.95, n=205 vs 194; Y3 6%, t(207)=2.32, p=.021, n=97 vs 116; Y4 7%, t(225)=2.20, p=.028. Raw Y1 Brier: none .42, trained .38.
limits: Effect shrank from 12% to 6-7% in later years; veterans carried over training. The paper's text and its table disagree on which Y4 group size is trained vs control.
agent_relevance: About 6 to 12% from one hour of instruction is a realistic expected gain, not a large one.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers & Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy
finding: Of the ten CHAMPS KNOW principles, only comparison classes (base rates) was reliably tied to better scores. Post-mortem (P) and O principle explanations were linked to worse scores, probably because they follow errors.
numbers: In Y4, 6,622 control explanations (75% of forecasters) and 6,714 trained ones (76%). 69% of trained explanations were self-classified under a principle. Only C, M and S forecasts beat unprincipled ones. ANOVA showed three significant principles; C best.
quote: The CHAMPS KNOW principle most associated with boosts in accuracy was the use of comparison classes and base-rates
limits: Self-reported principle use; assumes independence of explanations. Not a causal test of each principle.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the outside-view operator and base-rate anchor in the schema; nothing supports many other named heuristics.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers & Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy
finding: Cognitive ability and practice predict accuracy in all four years, but the predictors are weak. Raven's matrices was about zero; numeracy and CRT were better. Training had the largest coefficient. Motivation measures did not predict.
numbers: Table 11 standardized coefficients (Y1..Y4, negative is better): numeracy -.05,-.05,-.06,-.06; CRT -.07,-.04,-.02,-.02; Raven's -.02,-.01,.00,-.01; training -.10,-.14,-.09,-.16; AOMT -.02,-.04,-.05,.00; grit .03,.00,.03,n/a.
limits: Univariate coefficients only on standardized Brier. Different samples each year.
agent_relevance: Intervention beat trait. Engineering the procedure matters more than picking the 'smart' model.

source: Baron, Mellers, Tetlock, Stone & Ungar (2014) Two reasons to make aggregated probability forecasts more extreme
finding: Formal model of why averaged forecasts need extremizing: random error pushes a mean toward .5, and forecasters shrink their own estimates since they know they lack information. The transform is t(p)=p^a/(p^a+(1-p)^a).
numbers: GJP Year 1: 1,973 forecasters, 102 questions (86 used; 80 two-option). Mean number of questions per forecaster 47. High expertise: mean a=2.43, Brier .148 vs .187 untransformed; median a=1.78, .160 vs .176. Low expertise: mean a=3.08, .139 vs .196; median a=2.34, .153 vs .184.
limits: Fit in sample on one year. One 'a' per condition. Later work suggests the benefit may be unstable. Expert split was self-rated, per question median.
agent_relevance: Votes of copies of one model are correlated, so G4 bans extremizing them. Here the gain comes from diverse, partly informed people.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle & Ungar (2014) Combining probability forecasts and understanding probability extremizing through information diversity
finding: Partial-information model: experts share some information and hold other bits privately. The lower the overlap, the more the mean should be pushed out. Extremizing is more likely to help than hurt in non-trivial settings, but is not guaranteed.
numbers: Uses GJP as the example. States that every year the top 2% are chosen as superforecasters, base pay $150, leaderboard of top 20 by Brier. Proposition: extremizing can leave the convex hull of the forecasts.
limits: Mostly theory. Gaussian-information assumption; assumes experts are optimal given their own information.
agent_relevance: Same logic as G4: extremizing is justified only when sources hold different information. Copies hold the same.

source: Tetlock (2005) Expert Political Judgment
finding: Predecessor of GJP. Experts' long-term political forecasts were hardly better than simple baselines; 'foxes' beat 'hedgehogs'. Not opened this session; from memory of the standard summary.
numbers: About 284 experts and roughly 28,000 predictions over about 20 years (standard summary, not verified here).
limits: NOT READ. Do not cite numbers until checked. Superseded in method by the 2011-2015 tournaments with short time horizons.
agent_relevance: Source of the claim that style of thinking (many small ideas vs one big idea) matters. Compare to the schema's no-single-theory stance.

source: Tetlock & Gardner (2015) Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
finding: Popular account. Source of the 70% retention and .65 year-to-year correlation (p104, as cited by AI Impacts). Not opened this session.
numbers: Via AI Impacts: 70% and .65 on p104; modal superforecaster portrait; ten commandments.
limits: NOT READ. Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: The retention numbers should be checked against Mellers 2015 tables before they go into the schema.

source: Merkle, Petrov, Zhu, Karger, Tetlock & Himmelstein (2025) Identifying good forecasters via adaptive cognitive tests
finding: Item-response (beta) adaptive testing picks the most informative short cognitive tests to find good forecasters early, before questions resolve. Test scores stay strongly tied to forecasting in a second sample.
numbers: Study 1: 170 Facebook-recruited participants, 15 time-series questions each, 20 tests. Study 2: 1,194 participants, 36 questions, run about 8 months later; item parameters were stable between studies. Denominator Neglect was the most informative first test.
limits: Lay-person time-series questions, not geopolitics. Exact correlations with Brier not extracted (I read the abstract, methods and summaries only).
agent_relevance: Shows quick screening can approximate skill; for LLMs this is like cheap probes of a configuration before a full tournament.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han & Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Retrieval-augmented LM system (news search, reasoning prompts, trimmed-mean ensemble, fine-tuned on self-generated reasoning) nearly matches the crowd on a post-cutoff test set. Raw base LMs do not.
numbers: Dataset: 48,754 questions, 7.17M user forecasts from 5 platforms (2015-2024); test set from June 2023 on. Crowd Brier .149; system .179 (accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%); best zero-shot baseline GPT-4-1106 .208; random .25. Blending with crowd at 4x crowd weight: .146 vs .149.
limits: Crowd aggregates, not superforecasters. Later work (Paleka 2025) finds leakage risk in question selection (3.8% resolved early).
agent_relevance: Closest AI match to the GJP stack: retrieval, base rates, aggregation. Gains came from retrieval and fine-tuning, not from a clever prompt.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han & Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: System beats the crowd only when the crowd is unsure. It is weak when the crowd is certain, because the model hedges away from 0 and 1.
numbers: Crowd between .3 and .7: system .199 vs crowd .246 (validation); selective test setting .238 vs .240. Early retrieval dates: .185 vs .161 (crowd still better). At least 5 articles: .175 vs .143. All three conditions: .240 vs .247, 22% of forecasts. Where crowd is within .05 of 0 or 1: system accuracy +7% but Brier worse by .04. Calibration RMS error .42 (crowd .38).
limits: Selection rules found on validation; small gains within about 1.5 standard errors.
agent_relevance: Resolution gap again: LLMs lack sharpness at the extremes, the same point as superforecasters' high resolution.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han & Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Ablation shows where the gain comes from. Without fine-tuning and without retrieval the system falls back to baseline.
numbers: Full .179; no fine-tuning .186; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4 .182; no fine-tuning and no retrieval .206 (baseline .208). Fine-tune data: 13,253 samples kept only if they beat the crowd.
limits: Self-training on outputs filtered by the crowd's score may leak crowd info into the model.
agent_relevance: Information (retrieval) matters more than prompt wording, so an offline scaffold without search is capped near baseline.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Tuminauskaite & Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 different LLMs (median of models) matched a human crowd of 925 on 31 binary Metaculus questions. This is the LLM version of wisdom of crowds, with different models, not copies.
numbers: Preregistered: LLM crowd Brier M=.20 (SD .12) vs 50% baseline .25, t(30)=-2.35, p=.026. LLM crowd vs human crowd M=.19 (SD .19): t(60)=0.19, p=.850. Equivalence bounds d=.5 (0.081 Brier) satisfied, p=.017 and .040. Median LLM forecast 60%, so an acquiescence bias.
limits: Only 31 questions; wide equivalence bounds. Models overconfident and badly calibrated. The Metaculus questions were from a 3-month window.
agent_relevance: Diversity across models works; copies of one model do not (G4).

source: Schoenegger, Park, Tuminauskaite & Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: Study 2: showing the human median to GPT-4 and Claude 2 improved their Brier scores, but simple averaging of human and machine was better than the LLM updating alone.
numbers: GPT-4 .17 to .14 (p=.003); Claude 2 .22 to .15 (p<.001). Accuracy gain 17% to 28%. Update size correlated with distance to human median r=.88 (GPT-4) and .87 (Claude 2). Prediction intervals narrowed, GPT-4 17.75 to 14.22.
limits: Two models, one question set. Anchoring to a given number cannot be separated from learning.
agent_relevance: Code-level averaging beats asking the model to merge (schema G5).

source: Schoenegger & Park (2023) Large language model prediction capabilities: evidence from a real-world forecasting tournament
finding: Early test: GPT-4 entered in a Metaculus tournament (July to October 2023, 843 participants) did no better than always saying 50%, and far worse than the human crowd median.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier .20 (SD .18) vs human crowd median .07 (SD .08); difference .13, t(44)=3.11, p=.003, d=.94. Directionally correct: GPT-4 69.57% vs human crowd about 95%. Bayesian-model-average Brier .13 vs random, t(22)=-5.91.
limits: Small N (about 23 resolved questions in the main test). Single model, one prompt. Midpoint-clustering hypothesis not supported.
agent_relevance: Sets the baseline that later work improved on: raw prompting is not forecasting skill.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott & Tetlock (2024) AI-augmented predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting accuracy
finding: Humans with an LLM assistant forecast better, even if the assistant is noisy and overconfident. Not a persistence study, but it tests human skill with AI help.
numbers: N=991, six questions. Preregistered gain of 24% to 28% in accuracy over control (a weaker model with no numbers). Without one outlier item: superforecasting assistant +41%, noisy assistant +29%.
limits: Outlier-driven; control was a less capable model. Did not find that low-skill people gain more, or that crowd diversity dropped. I read the abstract and skimmed the rest.
agent_relevance: Even a bad advisor helps, so the value may be in forcing a considered number rather than the quality of advice.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Dynamic benchmark of 1,000 unresolved questions (no leakage). Superforecasters (39 recruited) beat both the public and the best LLM, with significance.
numbers: 200-question human subset: superforecasters Brier .096; public (500 people) .121; best LLM Claude 3.5 Sonnet .122 (p<.001 vs superforecasters). Best LLM without crowd freeze values .136. Combination questions: superforecasters .076, public .096, top LLM GPT-4o .130. Brier vs Chatbot Arena r=-.68, p=.003.
limits: Median of 39 superforecasters who could see each other's rationales for part of the 9-day run. Top LLMs had market crowd values for market questions.
agent_relevance: Gives the target: superforecaster level .096. Gap to LLM is about .026 on this set. Combination questions are a weak point.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on real-world forecasting against expert forecasters
finding: A year after earlier tests, frontier models passed the crowd baseline but still trailed a small group of expert forecasters on Metaculus.
numbers: 464 questions across two quarters. o3 Brier .1352 vs crowd .149 (Halawi) and .121 (Karger 2025). Ten expert forecasters on a 157-question subset: mean .1573 but median .0225 (SE .0189); text says experts .023 vs o3 .135. Five runs per question per model; o3-pro .1307 on hold-out.
limits: Mean .157 vs median .0225 differ greatly, so the distribution is skewed; the paper's expert claim relies on the median. Brier not comparable across question sets. Single author.
agent_relevance: Progress is real in about 12 months; the expert edge shows the gap is not just crowd averaging.

source: Paleka, Goel, Geiping & Tramer (2025) Pitfalls in evaluating language model forecasters
finding: Position paper: many LLM forecasting results are weakened by temporal leakage and by weak transfer to real forecasting. Gives checks.
numbers: At least 3.8% of Halawi et al's dataset resolved early (no forecasting needed). In Tao et al. (2025) at least 10% of questions were trivial given their cut date. Search results with date limits still leaked future items (example of a wrong-dated 'jan 6' result).
limits: Concerns, not a re-run with corrected scores. Does not give corrected Brier values.
agent_relevance: Treat any claim that an LLM equals superforecasters as unproven unless questions were truly unresolved at forecast time.

source: Cross-read: Lu (2025) noise argument with Himmelstein et al. (2021) split-half reliability
finding: Lu notes that with a 6.5% true Brier gap, a noisier forecaster still wins 24% of 50-question tournaments. Combined with Himmelstein's split-half r about .36-.41, one tournament season is a weak guide to skill for humans and models.
numbers: Lu: 6.5% gap, 50 questions, noisy forecaster wins 24% of the time. Himmelstein S1: same metric across 94-question halves r=.36 to .41.
limits: Cross-paper inference by me, not a published joint analysis.
agent_relevance: Our evaluation needs at least a few hundred questions per arm and repeated runs, else the 'persistence' is partly luck.
